prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

For James Richardson Gerard, juke-step Jerry, little wrestler, soul-mess of sinew and mind-sight, fired spark, joyed Jesuit, grief-clog too, but a Pan-flute in every Ave, you half-nelson the syntax dandies, ram them to canvas, sit upon and pin the god-fops, minions of ghost tomes, trite chimes, though you walk among them, too, jig and roar of black-robed stroll in golden-grove and choral iambs. You were, yes, that falcon flight, the labor, soar, and dive, but buzzard nose for carrion, too, sniffed your own, knew, alone, the rot, rope-knot or buckle of roots under-on rock, your gowned back to roses, rosaries, but eyes a song gone up, too, sickly little wings stuck in God-glue air: how long? You sang one dialectic flight, sir—the only kind. How high can the swallow swoop, how low the falcon grieve, relieve, in fall till pinions hold him, there, to kill? Light- weight, mutt, heaver of iron, scrap,feather: I believe the hurt, believe you saw what you saw.

# A Tribute to the Wrestling Soul

He was a small man, sinewy and taut, a soul forever locked in wrestling—not with others alone, but with himself, with language, and with God. In him joy and grief were never separate garments but a single woven cloth, and he wore them both at once. Grief did not diminish his joy, nor joy his grief; instead they grappled within him, each straining against the other, and out of that struggle came the strange music that was his alone.

Toward the conventional poets he was combative, impatient with those who merely imitated, who arranged their borrowed phrases in tidy, expected rows. He overpowered their syntax, broke it open, wrenched it into new and living shapes. The pretentious ones—those "god-fops" who paraded piety as ornament and wore faith like fashionable dress—he pinned down without mercy, exposing the hollowness beneath their polished surfaces.

His imagination took flight like a falcon, that magnificent bird of prey, soaring in wide arcs before folding its wings to plunge in sudden, breathtaking descent. There was ecstasy in that motion, in the sheer mastery of the dive. Yet he carried, too, a "buzzard nose"—a darker instinct that caught the scent of decay wherever it lingered. He smelled corruption in the world, and, unsparing, he smelled it in himself as well: the inner rot, the private failings, the slow spoiling of the flesh and spirit that no devotion could entirely hold back.

For he was torn, always torn. On one side stood his religious devotion: the rosaries told bead by bead, the gowned back bent in obedience, the prayers offered up in faithful repetition. On the other side strained a restless, yearning spirit that longed to rise and could not—like "sickly little wings stuck in God-glue air," beating and beating against a heaven that seemed at once to summon him and to hold him fast. His faith was not comfort but tension, a devotion that bound even as it lifted.

And so the speaker affirms his belief in this man—in the truth of his suffering and the authenticity of his vision. The pain was real, and so was the sight granted through it. This tribute does not smooth over the anguish or resolve the contradiction; it honors them. For it was precisely out of that torn and straining life that his singular "dialectic flight" was born—that soaring, diving, wrestling motion of a soul that could never rest, and that gave us, in its unrest, something rare and true.

# A Tribute to Gerard Manley Hopkins

You who wrenched the language from its sockets, who sprang the rhythm loose and let it buck against the traces—priest and poet both, you strained toward God through every fractured line, each stress a wrestling-hold, each dappled word a grappling with the Weight you could not name yet named a thousand ways. The falcon rides the buffeting wind of your imagining, the kestrel hangs and swings, its wings a metaphor for how the spirit lifts against what holds it down. You watched the windhover and saw the fire break from you, my chevalier, and something in that plunging flight was prayer, was ache, was praise.

They did not understand you, those who kept their measured feet and tidy couplets. You went alone into the difficult country of your own devising, hammering new music from old iron, forging syllables that clashed and rang like sparks struck off the anvil of your faith. What conventional ear could follow where you led? You bent the tongue to breaking, packed each phrase with more than phrases hold, and made a stubborn beauty out of your refusal to be ordinary.

But oh, the darkness in you—the terrible sonnets written in the trough of the wave, when God withdrew and left you clinging to the cliffs of your own mind. *No worst, there is none.* You knew the pitched past pitch of grief, the mountains of the mind, those cliffs of fall no man had fathomed. The very gift that lifted you also drove you down into the pit, and there you wrestled through the night with silence, with the fear that all your straining reached no ear at all.

And yet I will not doubt you. Whatever anguish tore you, whatever black hours pressed the breath from your belief, I trust the truth of what you suffered and the truth of what you saw. The pain was real. The vision was no lie. In the deep well of your torment there was still the water of authentic longing, and in your wildest, most contorted lines there beats a heart that would not stop believing—even when belief cost everything, even when it broke you. This is your testament, and I affirm it: the suffering was genuine, and so was the light you glimpsed beyond it.

# For James Richardson

There are people whose presence shapes the world around them quietly, and James Richardson was one of them. This text is written for him—not as a formal tribute, but as a genuine reflection on the kind of person worth remembering.

James Richardson carried himself with a calm confidence that put others at ease. Friends often described him as someone you could turn to in difficult moments, a person who listened more than he spoke, and who offered advice only when it was truly needed. For those who knew him well, his loyalty was never in question.

Throughout his life, James pursued his goals with quiet determination. He believed that hard work spoke louder than promises, and he built his reputation on consistency rather than grand gestures. Colleagues respected him for his fairness, and neighbors appreciated his willingness to lend a hand without being asked.

For anyone who crossed paths with James Richardson, the lesson was clear: kindness and dependability are worth more than fleeting recognition. He may not have sought the spotlight, but he earned something more lasting—the trust and affection of the people around him.

This is written for James Richardson, and for everyone who strives to live with the same quiet integrity he embodied.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem addressed to Gerard Manley Hopkins that echoes his sprung rhythm, compound coinages, and imagery of the windhover, wrestling with faith and despair.
counterfactuals.output:
# Letter to the Priest Who Made Words Kneel

Gerard, God-grieved and glory-galled, I write you across the century-chasm, you dapple-souled watcher of the morning's minion—

That bird you caught, that dawn-drawn dauphin of the air-kingdom, still hovers hungering above my own gray gutter-days. I have seen him: wind-walker, thermal-riding, the buckle-and-break of him, the fire that folds from a thing when it does the deed it was dovetailed for. You knew. You knew the way a kestrel and a Christ can share one syllable of shine.

But you knew also the other thing—the cliff-fall inward, the no-worst-there-is-none nights, the mind's mountains where a man hangs cheap by his own fraying. I know them too, Father Hopkins, heart-hoarder, hope-hollowed. The pitched-past-pitch of grief. The comfortless comfort that will not come though we cry and cry and the wall gives back only wall.

How did you hold them both—the windhover's wild yes and the widow-dark of God's long silence? You, the wine-pressed, world-mothering-mind man, dying in a Dublin you did not love, ash-mouthed, fever-thinned, and still the last words gladness-galled: *I am so happy, I am so happy.*

Teach me that dapple. Teach me the sprung and stubborn scansion of a soul that stresses joy where the meter would let it rest. Show me how the self can be its own dark-mothing candle and still throw light. For I too walk the wan waste, I too watch the empty east—

and yet the bird. And yet the bird still climbs.

And yet the fire, blue-bleak, breaks brilliant from the ember when we, hard-fallen, gall ourselves and gash and go on gold-vermilion.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental tribute to a tormented Jesuit poet, using hyphenated word-fusions, bird imagery (falcon, swallow, buzzard), and a tone of both admiration and anguish.
counterfactuals.output:
**Windhover-Haunted: A Tribute to Gerard Manley Hopkins**

*i.*

You—priest-clenched, God-grieved, ink-starved man,
your falcon still rides the morning-minted air,
that dapple-dawn-drawn dauphin of the wind,
wing-buckled, blade-bright, terror-tender there—
oh how you caught it! how the buckle-flame
broke gold-vermilion from the plodding plough,
and made the sillion shine. I say your name
and stumble in the swallow-swift of *now*.

*ii.*

But under-song, the buzzard-shadow came,
slow-circling, patience-cruel, the carrion-clock
that ticked above your cloister-narrowed bed.
No falcon-lift for you in those wan hours—
only the cliff-fall of the mind, the sheer
no-worst, the pitched-past-pity precipice-year,
where comfort served no comfort, and the dead
selfyeast of spirit soured the sour-dark flour.

*iii.*

Swallow-swift, falcon-fierce, then buzzard-low—
the three-fold bird of you: the up, the ache, the down.
I mourn your mercy-hungering, God-withheld,
your letters loosed like feathers no one crowned.
You buried genius in the ash-heap years,
combustion hidden, wildfire-under-stone,
and burned unwitnessed, self-consumed, alone,
a match-flare quenched in Ireland's grief-grey rain.

*iv.*

Yet—here's the mercy the dumb centuries kept:
the ash relit. Your dead-hoard leaps to living,
inscape unlocked, each stress-sprung syllable
a resurrection-riff, a plume, a giving.
Not buzzard-eaten after all, but flown—
world-wide, wind-borne, your falcon-fire re-thrown.
Poor tortured Father, gerard-glad and grave:
you sank like larks—to rise. You lost—to save.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: In the style of Gerard Manley Hopkins, write a dense, muscular apostrophe celebrating his poetry, wrestling metaphors, and his struggle between religious devotion and inner rot.
counterfactuals.output:
**To Hopkins, Grappling**

O grip-fist God-wrestler, gaunt-throated Gerard! how you hauled
the heaved-up word, wrung-out, wrung-wet, and wrote it wracked —
you, tackle-tongued, tough-tender, thew-and-sinew-souled,
who caught the kingfisher's *catch*, the dapple-dawn-drawn fact,
    the very *inscape* instressed and grace-galled!

Praise! for the plunge of it, the sprung and sprinting stress,
the buckle-and-break where beauty's *behold!* bells clear —
Christ-play in ten thousand places, limb-lit loveliness,
the world charged, chrism-charged, oil-oozed, and shining sheer,
    while you, poor priest, went pressed and prayer-oppressed.

For here's the harrow, here the halting, hidden thing:
you, God's own gaunt-cheeked grinder, gall-grubbed, gut-gnawn,
who felt the *fell of dark, not day* come cowling —
the self-yeast souring, the spirit's sweating dawn
    where no dawn dared, no dear-lit larkspur wing.

You, dead-letter'd, dungeon'd, dark-diving deep,
crying *I wake and feel* — the fell, the cliff-of-fall,
mind-mountains sheer, no-man-fathomed, terror-steep,
where the worm of self went winding through it all,
    rot in the root while the branch bore blossom's leap.

And *this* the miracle, this the wrestled won:
that out of decay you dredged the diamond-durance line,
that gall could gild, that ash could *ah!* the sun,
that Christ, at compass-point of your comfortless sign,
    held — *hand* against the hollow, undone, undone —

so pitch and praise contended, plied, and pressed,
your black hour bearing bloom, your groan a *gash of gold*.
O most-tormented, most-transfigured, God's own guest
at his own famished feast — you took the terrible hold
    and would not loose it, *would not*, till you were blessed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

**To the Priest Who Boxed His God**

Hopkins, hard-knuckled, hush now—hear me, huntsman of the hidden:
you jabbed, you jarred, you grappled grief-grabbed against the gaunt
unanswering Arm. O anvil-hearted, altar-thrown, you pinned
what would not pin, you clinched the cloud, you counted out the count

of nights not-numbered, no bell, no breath, no break. Bruise-black
the round rolls on. Doubt is a low blow, brother; doubt drops
its dead-weight in the wrestler's throat. Did He *lock* you back,
or was it your own arm, ache-anointed, that would not stop?

Ropes ring the ringless. Who cornered whom? The crowd was cold.
You bled a psalm, spit-bright, and bowed—not beaten, not blessed—
your face a fist God clenched then loosed, unfold, unfold,
un**held**. Say if the grip was love, or only the last

thing left to grip. Say. Or don't. The gong is grief. Go, ground-
grazed grace, go dark, go doubt-wrung, glory-gouged, unrenowned.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a modernist elegy or address to "James Richardson Gerard" that plays on The Windhover, uses invented compound words, and captures a soul torn between grace and grief.
counterfactuals.output:
# To James Richardson Gerard

*after Hopkins*

I caught this morning morning's-mourner, the dawn-drawn
   Kestrel of your keeping, king-souled in the grey-gilt air,
   riding the rolling level underneath him steady-there—
how he hung, heart-hinged, on the wimpling wind's-brawn!

Then off, off forth on swing, a soul-sprung, sorrow-sawn
   arc—as a skater's heel sweeps bow-bend, buoyant, bare—
   the hurl and gliding both! My grief-goaded heart in hiding, spare
me the stir, the striving stung by beauty, brute and brawn.

O Gerard-ghost, grace-grieved: here Buckle! and the fire
   that breaks from you then, billion-fold brighter, blood-bequeathed,
   no wonder of it: shéer plód makes plough down sillion shine,
and blue-bleak embers, ah my dear, fall-gall'd, expire,
   gash gold-vermilion—so your gashed name, unwreathed,
   flames from the fallow, father, faltering, forever mine.

---

*A note on the making:* The poem borrows the falcon-flight of Hopkins's octave and the "Buckle!"-turn of his volta, but bends the ecstasy toward loss. The invented compounds—*morning's-mourner*, *soul-sprung*, *sorrow-sawn*, *grace-grieved*, *blood-bequeathed*, *fall-gall'd*—hold the two poles together, each word a hinge where grace and grief refuse to part.
